subject: CJS model estimating lower than expected survival

messages.author: a2bfdf24157fa01a
messages.subject: CJS model estimating lower than expected survival
parts:
Hello,

I have used the CJS model in the manual as a starting point for a mark recapture analysis, but I am getting some unexpected results, and I am not sure why. The basic setup is the animals are marked at t = 1, and then "recaptured" at intervals t with detection probability p. The model is basically taken straight from the manual (v2.14 pp 212-215).

The issue is the estimated survival from the model is lower than the observed frequency at all time-points. I would expect the other way around, given that imperfect detection probabilities.  A possible explanation is the detection and survival probabilities are pretty high, so uncertainty in the estimates is skewed (i.e., the estimates are bounded on the upper end at 1). Propagated over the 15 intervals, this leads to survival estimates lower than observed in all cases? 

I was wondering if this was expected behavior or if something funny was happening. The model and data are attached.

Thanks,

Matt

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] CJS model estimating lower than expected survival
parts:
I have no idea about this particular model, but what you want
to do is simulate data according to the model and see if you can
fit it.

Yes, you can run into problems fitting, but you should be getting
warnings. If you're running in RStan, they're probably hidden on
multiple chains and then you'll need to look up this to figure
out how to diagnose:

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/vignettes/stanfit-objects.html

We're working on Stan 3 and I hope we can make a lot of this
diagnostic stuff more seamless.

- Bob

messages.author: a2bfdf24157fa01a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] CJS model estimating lower than expected survival
parts:
Thanks for the advice, Bob.

I did as you suggested, and overall the model performs well for the simulated data across different parameters of survival and detection.

For those interested, we think we have identified something that might be causing the discrepancies: the model assumes independent p(survive), while knowledge of the system suggest an animal that survives through the initial sampling period likely has greater fitness and will survive the entire time. We are working to adjust the model accordingly.

Thanks again for your help,

Matt

Cool! I love it when science happens.

You get the same kind of data when you look at patients
surviving in a clinical study. I'm not sure how the epidemiologists
handle it other than by hierarchical modeling of individuals.

It's much easier to concentrate on where the problem
is if you've eliminated things like bugs in the code.

- Bob
